newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Kuwait aims to raise oil sales to new markets.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait aims to raise oil sales to new markets.

text.p: State-owned Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC) aims to expand its oil product sales to Asian countries which it has not yet penetrated in order to soak up its higher refining capacity, KPC officials said on Tuesday.

"We are targetting to expand our supplies to all countries in Asia such as Sri Lanka and Bangladesh as well as Laos, Cambodia, Burma and China," Sulaiman Al-Najdi, manager in KPC's representative office in Singapore told Reuters.
KPC also wants to boost sales to Indonesia and Vietnam, where it already has a strong presence, he said. More than 70 percent of Kuwait's total refining output is exported to Asia, Al-Najdi said.
Kuwait National Petroleum Co (KNPC), KPC's refining arm, plans to raise domestic capacity to 900,000 barrels per day at the beginning of 1998 from around 895,000 bpd in February.
It plans to raise this to one million bpd by 2000 by building a 100,000-bpd crude distillation unit at Shuaiba, the oil-rich Gulf state's smallest refinery which now has a 155,000-bpd capacity.
KPC is planning 400,000 bpd in refining capacity in Asia, starting with joint ventures in India, Pakistan and Thailand.
It is in the early stages of evaluating the possibility of building refineries in Indonesia and China, but no decision has been made yet, KPC executives said.
The higher refining capacity is consistent with Kuwait's plan to raise crude output from its current OPEC supply quota of two million bpd to 2.5 million by 2000 and three million by 2005.
KPC will open a representative office in New Delhi this year in pursuit of a bigger slice of the vast Indian market when the country opens its internal market, industry sources said.

Kuwait now exports about 900,000 tonnes of diesel and 1.08 million tonnes of kerosene a year to India on term contracts. It supplies 75 percent of Pakistan's annual diesel, kerosene and fuel oil requirements.
To get a slice of the Bangladesh market, a KPC sales team will visit Dhaka in two weeks to assess the terms of its annual import tenders and requirements.
Al-Najdi said Bangladesh oil product imports were now about 800,000 tonnes for six months and were growing steadily.
He said KPC preferred term contracts of up to five years to ensure stability of production and delivery and so refineries and the shipping fleet can plan ahead and contain costs.
Supply stability is also a prerequisite for customers such as Indonesia and Vietnam, which view term deals as a way of protectiion from the volatile spot market.
For example Indoil, a trading affiliate of national oil company Pertamina, recently sealed a new term contract with KPC to supply 55,000 tonnes of jet fuel every 40 days.
KPC also sells 80,000 tonnes of diesel a month to Indonesia under an annual term deal, while another 500,000 tonnes a year of oil products are sold through spot sales.
Vietnam also raised its term purchase of diesel from Kuwait to 700,000 tonnes from 500,000 tonnes a year and up to 130,000 tonnes of jet fuel from 80,000 tonnes.

KPC seeks to boost its presence to the rest of Indochina in anticipation of booming economies. Cambodia's annual diesel and gasoline imports are 600,000-700,000 tonnes with demand projected to grow at 10 percent a year, the executives said.
